segments.text: Every Sunday evening, around seven or eight o'clock,
a strange feeling quietly settles into millions of living rooms.
You are still off work.
You are sitting on your couch, nobody is asking for a spreadsheet,
and yet, your chest tightens just a little bit
because tomorrow is Monday.
And Monday means five straight days of trading your waking hours
for two days left over at the end.
Ah, five days on, two days off.
Most of us treat it like a law of nature,
like seven days in a week or 24 hours in a day.
And if you ask people why we do it this way,
they usually tell you the same story.
They say life used to be an endless, brutal grind
that our ancestors worked from sunrise to sunset every day
just to survive,
and that the five-day work week is the pinnacle of modern progress.
That is the official story.
There is just one problem with it.
When historians opened the tax ledgers,
parish calendars, and court records
of the pre-industrial world,
they found the exact opposite.
In 1991, Harvard economist Juliet Shor
examined the work records of 14th century English peasants.
These were people living under feudal lords
with no tractors, no electricity, and no labor laws.
And yet, in a typical year,
a medieval peasant worked roughly 150 days,
not 260 days like a modern office worker, 150.
Between winter lulls, harvest pauses,
and over 100 parish feast days,
medieval laborers spent nearly half the year
not working for their lord at all.
Even on work days,
the day was broken up by long midday meals,
afternoon naps, and ale breaks.
So how did a species with power grids,
computers, and time-saving machines
end up locked inside a stricter schedule
than a 14th century peasant?
To find out, you have to trace a 300-year war
over something you carry in your pocket every day.
The clock.
For almost all of human history,
people did not work by the hour.
They worked by the task.
If you were a cobbler, a blacksmith,
or a weaver in the 1700s,
your rhythm was bursts of effort
followed by long stretches of rest.
You worked hard when an order came in,
or when the harvest was ripe.
And when the job was done, you stopped.
Across England and early America,
artisans even had a weekly tradition
that drove early business owners crazy.
They called it Saint Monday.
Sunday was for church, family, and the tavern,
which meant Monday was for recovering from Sunday.
Workshops stood half empty on Mondays.
Many weavers did not touch their looms
until Tuesday afternoon,
working late on Thursday and Friday to finish their quota.
Time belonged to the person doing the work
until the steam engine changed the rules.
A hand loom can sit quiet on a Monday morning
without costing a penny.
A massive coal-powered factory cannot.
Every hour those iron machines stood cold
was money burning in the furnace.
As historian E.P. Thompson documented in 1967,
the Industrial Revolution was not just a revolution in machines.
It was a revolution in human discipline.
Factory owners needed human bodies that behaved like gears,
showing up at the exact same minute six days a week.
In many early textile mills,
workers were forbidden from carrying pocket watches.
Only the master clock on the factory wall
was allowed to tell the time,
and mill owners routinely slowed the clock down during the shift,
so workers stayed 30 minutes longer without knowing it.
Saint Monday was crushed with heavy fines.
Parish feast days were wiped off the calendar.
By the 1850s, the new normal across Europe and America
was six full days a week, 12 hours a day,
with only Sunday left to catch your breath.
People did not evolve toward working more.
They were forced into a six-day cage in a single generation.
So how did Saturday finally break free from that six-day cage?
Most textbooks give the credit to one man, Henry Ford.
On September 25th, 1926,
Ford stunned the business world by announcing that his workers
would now work only five days a week,
Monday through Friday, for the same six-dollar daily pay.
On the surface, it looked like extraordinary generosity.
The head of U.S. Steel warned that giving workers two whole days off
would destroy the moral fabric of America.
Wait, stop right there.
Henry Ford was one of the most ruthless efficiency obsessives in history.
He had a private security force that spied on his workers
to make sure they were not slacking off.
He did not give away millions of hours of labor out of kindness.
He had discovered a fatal math problem at the heart of capitalism.
By the mid-1920s, Ford's assembly lines were churning out
Model T cars faster than ever.
His workers even earned enough to afford one.
There was just one catch.
Why would a man buy a family car if he worked six days a week,
collapsed into bed on Saturday night, and spent his only day off in church on Sunday?
A worker who is always working has no time to be a customer.
Listen to what Henry Ford told World's Work magazine in 1926,
right after announcing the five-day week.
People who have more leisure must have more clothes.
They must have a greater variety of food.
They must have more transportation facilities.
This increased consumption will require greater production than we now have.
Read that again.
Saturday was not given back so you could sit under a tree like an ancient hunter-gatherer.
Saturday was invented so you would have time to go shopping.
One day for rest on Sunday.
One day to spend your paycheck on Saturday.
And five days to earn it all back again.
And here is the part of the story almost nobody gets taught in school.
In the 1930s, nobody believed the five-day 40-hour week was the final destination.
Everybody thought it was just a temporary stop on the way down.
In 1930, economist John Maynard Keynes calculated that with technology advancing so fast,
his grandchildren would only need to work about 15 hours a week — maybe three hours a day.
And in April 1933, at the height of the Great Depression,
the U.S. Senate actually voted on a bill introduced by Senator Hugo Black.
The bill made it illegal for any factory or business to employ someone for more than
30 hours a week, six hours a day, five days a week.
And it passed the U.S. Senate, 53 to 30.
Kellogg's even switched its battle creek plant to six-hour shifts and found that accidents dropped,
efficiency rose, and workers had the entire afternoon free.
For a few months in 1933, the six-hour workday was on the verge of becoming the law of the land.
Then came a wave of corporate lobbying.
Business leaders warned President Roosevelt that if workers tasted 30 hours a week,
they would never go back.
The bill was buried in the house.
Five years later, in 1938, the Fair Labor Standards Act locked the counter at 40 hours across five days.
And then the clock simply froze.
Since 1938, the productivity of an American worker has increased by over 300 percent.
A task that took a room of clerks a week in 1940 now takes a spreadsheet four seconds.
By every law of math, Keynes should have been right.
We should be leaving our desks on Tuesday afternoon.
So why are you still sitting there at 501 on a Friday?
In 1955, historian Cyril Northcoat Parkinson wrote a famous line in The Economist.
Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.
When society moved from factory floors to office desks,
we stopped measuring work by what you produce and kept measuring it by how many days your chair is warm.
If a five-hour task is given 40 hours of office time,
it grows meetings, reports, and email chains until it takes all 40 hours.
Anthropologist David Graber found that millions of office workers admit they could finish their
real work in 15 to 20 hours a week.
Almost the exact same 17 hours recorded among Kalahari hunter-gatherers.
The rest of the week is spent performing the ritual of being busy.
And the extra welfare machines created?
Instead of trading it for Tuesday and Wednesday off,
our economy taught us to trade it for bigger houses,
newer phones, and faster subscriptions.
Things that require five days of paycheck to maintain.
The five-day work week is not an ancient human law.
It is barely 90 years old.
It was born from steam engines,
polished by a carmaker who needed weekend shoppers,
and frozen in 1938.
Which makes that tightness in your chest on Sunday night look very different.
Your body isn't broken for dreading a 40-hour fluorescent box.
Your body is just remembering how human time used to work.
